title: Bio & health: Alzheimer's atlases, AI's evidence gap, and a rare-disease approval
summary: The day's research feed leaned toward neurobiology and evidence quality: new Alzheimer's disease models and cohorts, a first-in-human amygdala ultrasound trial, and a set of papers and commentary on how AI should be evaluated before it reaches patients. A gene therapy for an ultra-rare disease and a broad trial pipeline filled out the rest. Nothing here is medical advice.

stories.headline: A lifespan single-cell atlas of the human developing hippocampus benchmarks familial Alzheimer's disease brain organoids.
stories.dek: New disease models, an Amish cohort study and an analysis of repurposing candidates all point at the same target from different directions.
tldr: A bioRxiv preprint presents a lifespan single-cell atlas of the developing human hippocampus as a benchmark for familial Alzheimer's disease brain organoids.
A second preprint, BRIDGE-AD, reports Alzheimer's disease effectors through interpretable integration of large-scale omics data.
A medRxiv study examines heritability and rare-variant contributions to Alzheimer disease in the Midwestern Amish, and another analyzes varenicline as a repurposable candidate for ADRD prevention.

body.text: A bioRxiv preprint describes a lifespan single-cell atlas of the human developing hippocampus intended to benchmark familial Alzheimer's disease brain organoids. A separate bioRxiv preprint, BRIDGE-AD, says it reveals Alzheimer's disease effectors through interpretable large-scale omics integration. Both are preprints and have not completed peer review.

Population genetics is the second strand. A medRxiv study quantifies heritability and rare-variant contributions to Alzheimer disease in the Midwestern Amish, and a companion medRxiv analysis follows age-related traits and cognitive function in the Collaborative Amish Aging and Memory Project.

Treatment hypotheses appear as computational work rather than trial results. One medRxiv analysis evaluates varenicline as a repurposable drug candidate for ADRD prevention, and a summary in the science-news feed describes research on whether some blood thinners may have an unexpected benefit for Alzheimer's patients.

stories.whyItMatters: Alzheimer's drug development has repeatedly failed in late-stage trials, which raises the value of better disease models and of separating genuine causal signals from observational associations. The day's output is model- and cohort-building work that later trials depend on.
stories.editorNote: All items here are preprints or headline-level summaries without peer review, so confidence is medium and no effect sizes are reported because the collection does not include abstracts.

stories.headline: Artificial intelligence in clinical trials-state of the evidence, gaps, and next steps
stories.dek: Papers on AI in trials, patient-facing generative AI and a geriatrician's commentary converge on evaluation as the binding constraint.
tldr: A PubMed review examines the state of the evidence for AI in clinical trials, its gaps and next steps.

Related papers evaluate patient-facing generative AI and an AI preoperative planning system for high tibial osteotomy; an ISPOR task force reports good practices for generative AI in systematic reviews.
A STAT commentary argues AI for older adults deserves careful scrutiny.

body.text: A PubMed review titled "Artificial intelligence in clinical trials-state of the evidence, gaps, and next steps" surveys where AI has been used in trials and where the evidence is thin. A second paper studies the interpretive influence and system-level evaluation of patient-facing generative AI, shifting scrutiny from model accuracy to how patients read its output.

Applied evaluations continue in surgical and evidence-synthesis settings. One study reports that an AI-based preoperative planning system for high tibial osteotomy significantly enhances planning speed with accuracy comparable to surgeons, and an ISPOR special task force sets out good practices for using generative AI in systematic literature reviews.

Commentary in the science and health press adds a population-specific caution. A STAT piece argues that AI for older adults deserves careful scrutiny, as told by a geriatrician, focusing on where deployment assumptions may not hold for that group.

stories.whyItMatters: AI is entering care through trials, patient-facing tools and evidence synthesis at once. The recurring finding across these items is that evaluation design, not model capability, determines whether the tooling helps.
stories.editorNote: Abstracts are not stored in the collection, so each item is described from its title and venue; no specific performance figures are asserted beyond the wording of the titles.

stories.headline: STAT+: FDA approves a new gene therapy for Sanfilippo syndrome, an ultra-rare disease
stories.dek: An approval for an ultra-rare disease arrived alongside preclinical gene-therapy work and a review of CRISPR-based biosensors.
tldr: STAT reported that the FDA approved a new gene therapy for Sanfilippo syndrome, described as an ultra-rare disease.
A bioRxiv preprint reports that neonatal AAV-SIL1 gene therapy prevents Marinesco-Sjogren syndrome in mice.
A PubMed review covers signal transduction and engineering strategies for CRISPR-Cas biosensors.

body.text: The FDA approved a new gene therapy for Sanfilippo syndrome, according to STAT, which frames the condition as ultra-rare. The collection carries the approval at headline level, without label details, trial data or pricing.

Preclinical work in the same feed covers a related modality: a bioRxiv preprint reports that neonatal AAV-SIL1 gene therapy prevents Marinesco-Sjogren syndrome in mice, a mouse-model result that has not been evaluated in humans.
On the platform side, a PubMed review examines signal transduction and engineering strategies for CRISPR-Cas biosensors, a diagnostic rather than therapeutic use of gene-editing tools.

stories.whyItMatters: Approvals in ultra-rare disease validate gene therapy as a commercial pathway even for very small patient populations, while the preclinical and biosensor items show the platform widening into new diseases and into diagnostics.
stories.editorNote: This is a headline-level approval report; the collection contains no clinical data, so the story states the approval and the adjacent research without extrapolating outcomes.

stories.headline: Low-Intensity Focused Ultrasound of the Amygdala in Depression and Anxiety: A First-in-Human Active-Controlled Trial
stories.dek: A first-in-human neuromodulation trial overlaps with basic work on how amygdala neurons join valence-related ensembles and with a developmental study of anxiety.
tldr: A medRxiv preprint reports a first-in-human, active-controlled trial of low-intensity focused ultrasound of the amygdala in depression and anxiety.
A bioRxiv preprint studies how basolateral amygdala neurons await oscillatory recruitment into valence-relevant ensembles.
A second medRxiv study replicates a developmental pathway to anxiety moderated by neural responsivity to unexpected stimuli.

body.text: A medRxiv preprint describes a first-in-human, active-controlled trial of low-intensity focused ultrasound aimed at the amygdala in depression and anxiety. As a preprint, it has not completed peer review, and the collection does not include its results.

The basic-science counterpart is a bioRxiv preprint on how basolateral amygdala neurons await oscillatory recruitment into valence-relevant ensembles, describing a mechanism by which the same region assigns emotional significance.

Developmental work extends the theme. A second medRxiv study reports a community-sample replication of a pathway to anxiety moderated by neural responsivity to unexpected stimuli in early infancy and childhood.

stories.whyItMatters: Focused ultrasound is being tested as a non-invasive alternative for psychiatric conditions where existing options fail many patients. Pairing an early human trial with mechanistic and developmental work shows how the same circuit is approached from several directions.
stories.editorNote: The trial is a preprint reporting a first-in-human study; the collection carries no outcome data, so the story describes the design and adjacent research without claiming efficacy.

stories.headline: 8 common food additives linked to high blood pressure and heart disease
stories.dek: Observational diet research and two cardiovascular studies on gut microbiota and on religiosity add to the evidence base without settling causation.
tldr: A science-news summary reports eight common food additives linked to high blood pressure and heart disease.
A medRxiv study uses machine learning to identify gut-microbiota biomarkers in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction and primary ventricular tachyarrhythmias.
Another medRxiv analysis examines the mixed impact of religiosity and spirituality on cardiovascular risk over time.

body.text: A science-news item reports that eight common food additives have been linked to high blood pressure and heart disease. The linkage described is observational and does not by itself establish that the additives cause the outcomes.

Two medRxiv preprints add cardiovascular data. One applies machine learning to identify gut-microbiota biomarkers in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction who presented with primary ventricular tachyarrhythmias; the other examines how religiosity and spirituality track with cardiovascular risk over time in a mixed direction.

stories.whyItMatters: Cardiovascular risk is shaped by diet, the microbiome and social factors simultaneously. These items are associative studies that generate hypotheses; none is a controlled trial of an intervention.
stories.editorNote: Observational and preprint material only; the collection has no abstracts, so no effect sizes are cited and causation is not implied.

stories.headline: AI DErived Plaque Quantification: CCTA and AI-QCPA for Determining Effective CAD Management
stories.dek: New and updated registry entries spanned AI cardiac imaging, a supplement trial, metabolic and oncology studies, and an AI review of diabetes self-management.
tldr: ClinicalTrials.gov entries in the collection include a trial of AI-derived plaque quantification from CCTA imaging for coronary artery disease management.
Other registry entries cover Urolithin A supplementation and glucose metabolism in adults 55 and older, and proton therapy for small cell lung cancer.
A PubMed scoping review covers AI-driven digital tools for diabetes self-management in children.

body.text: The registry feed carried a study titled "AI DErived Plaque Quantification: CCTA and AI-QCPA for Determining Effective CAD Management," grouping an imaging-derived biomarker with a management decision in coronary artery disease. A separate entry evaluates intensity-modulated proton therapy for small cell lung cancer.

Interventional and supplement studies fill out the pipeline. One randomized, triple-masked controlled trial examines the effects of Urolithin A supplementation on glucose metabolism in healthy adults aged 55 and older; another entry tests ultrasound-guided needle percutaneous electrolysis with therapeutic exercise in femoroacetabular impingement syndrome.

A PubMed scoping review takes a different angle, surveying AI-driven digital tools for diabetes self-management in children. Registry entries describe planned or ongoing work, so they are not results.

stories.whyItMatters: Trial registrations are an early signal of where a field is heading before results exist. This snapshot shows AI moving into routine imaging decisions while conventional device, supplement and radiotherapy studies continue.
stories.editorNote: Registry entries are study descriptions, not outcomes; titles are reported as registered and no results or effect sizes are asserted.
